messages.subject: interpretation of half-normal detection function
parts:
Hi all,

 

I’m using a half-normal detection function for fitting an secr model to a capture/re-capture dataset for a rare canid species using trap-type ‘single’. Thanks to all your help in this google group and the wonderful secr online documentation, I am making progress and am now getting reasonable results! However, I’m still unclear on what exactly the parameters (g0 and sigma) mean for the detection function. As an example, I’ve included a picture of the detection function shown in the secr-tutorial pdf. Can someone shed some light on how to interpret this? In particular, what does it mean when g0 is really small (as in this example)? Also, how is the this curve calculated? Is it based strictly on recaptures within the data?

 

Thanks kindly and looking forward to hearing from you,

 

Laura

messages.author: 118cea91a1619106
messages.subject: Re: interpretation of half-normal detection function
parts:
Hi Laura
The detection function describes the probability that an individual will be detected at a particular detector on a particular occasion. The further apart are the animal's activity centre and the detector, the lower the probability. Animal activity centres are not observed, and distances are not observed; all we have are detection histories (patterns) of observed individuals, but these are sufficient to fit the (implicit) model by maximising the likelihood. As you suggest, this is based on recaptures within the data, in that detection histories with multiple observations provide information on the spatial scale of detection (sigma). The parameters g0 and sigma jointly define the detection function. It's common for g0 to be small - remember it relates to a single detector on a single occasion.
Murray

messages.subject: RE: interpretation of half-normal detection function
parts:
Hi Murray,

 

As always, thank you for the response! Good to know that it is common for g0 to be small – that makes me feel better.

 

After some more investigation, I adjusted the spacing of the mask I was using and realized that it makes quite a difference in my results (before I was just using the default spacing from make.mask). I’m finding that the smaller I make the spacing, the larger the density estimate. I noticed that the SPACECAP manual suggests using 1/32 of a home range for pixel area to determine the spacing. Do you think that is reasonable, or is there another way that you would suggest to determine the spacing for the mask? Should it converge at some point, at which then we would know it is sufficiently small?

 

Now that I have adjusted the spacing of the mask, the probability surface from pdot.contour looks odd. Specifically, several of the trap lines do not have any contour lines around them (pic attached). It does not seem to be related to the # of captures/recaptures since some of the trap lines that had no captures still have contour lines around them. Could you help me understand why some trap lines have contours and others do not? Is it something that I should be concerned about?

 

Much appreciated and looking forward to hearing from you,

 

Laura

messages.author: 118cea91a1619106
messages.subject: Re: interpretation of half-normal detection function
parts:
See secr-habitatmasks.pdf for discussion of mask spacing (pixel size). Certainly you need to set the spacing with care when using clustered detectors. 1/32 HR size is probably not too far out, but you need to confirm that using plots like Fig. 5 in the pdf.

There is not enough information to diagnose your contour problem. Increase nx in pdot.contour for a prettier picture (e.g., nx=128 or nx=256).

Murray

messages.author: 0dbfcf0efe4ff8fe
messages.subject: Re: interpretation of half-normal detection function
parts:
Good day Laura,
If, when you reduced spacing, you didn't increase the total number of points in the mask, then the extent of the mask will shrink.  If the extent of the mask is too small, density estimates will be sensitive to the extent. Make sure you're keeping the extent the same when you reduce spacing (which perhaps you are; this is just a guess as to what might have happenned).
Eric
